steps.question: Why does monotone decrease alone not guarantee that minimum?
steps.answer_text: Decrease controls each outcome separately, but not the optimum of the probability-weighted sum under sum_i q_i = 1; a decreasing loss can therefore prefer Q different from P.
steps.why: This follows by general constrained-optimization knowledge applied to the average-loss formula in t001423.jpg and the target condition in t001456.jpg: at an interior optimum p_i f'(q_i) must be equal across i, a condition not implied merely by f'(x) < 0.

answer: The three non-logarithmic candidates are f(x) = 1/x - 1, f(x) = tan((pi/2)(1-x)), and f(x) = Gamma(x) - 1. Their being decreasing only says that assigning more probability to the outcome that occurs gives that outcome a smaller individual loss. The actual requirement is stronger: the weighted average sum_i p_i f(q_i), with the q_i coupled by sum_i q_i = 1, must attain its minimum at Q = P. Monotonicity alone does not control that coupled tradeoff, so a decreasing candidate can have its optimum at Q != P. Equivalently, an interior optimum requires p_i f'(q_i) to be the same for all i; demanding q_i = p_i for every P forces x f'(x) to be constant (the logarithmic form, up to scale and an additive constant), which the three candidates do not satisfy.
